KEY MESSAGE 1...Isolated to scattered showers and thunderstorms 
possible this afternoon with the greatest risk for western 
southern New England.

Today will be of a transition day between the dry weekend and the 
upcoming wet pattern. Much of the day will feature dry conditions 
and mainly sunny skies with highs in the low to mid 80s for the in 
interior and mid to upper 70s for the coastal areas. Low clouds
will continue to scatter of the Cape and Islands this morning 
as an offshore low pressure system continues to pull further 
away. A mid- level trough positions over the region ahead of an 
embedded shortwave tracking across the Great Lakes region. Flow 
becomes more southerly later in the day with moisture advecting 
in. Instability builds across west and central southern New 
England ahead of the wave with the help of daytime heating with 
MLCAPE values 500-1200 J/kg. This should support development of 
afternoon/evening showers and thunderstorms. Mid-level lapse 
rates and shear are in little to marginal values which will 
favor more pulse storms rather than severe. With the stronger 
forcing further west, the coverage will be more limited as well 
(isolated to scattered). The greatest risk of a shower or 
thunderstorms today will be for western southern New England. 
Due to the lower coverage nature probabilities are on the lower 
end (15-30%) for these areas. There is a low chance (< 10%) for 
a stray shower/storm to make into central MA/CT. With 
precipitable water values rising to 1.0-1.25" in the afternoon, 
can't rule out a brief downpour with any storms alongside the 
lightning risk. 

Any remaining showers or storms diminish tonight. Moisture continues 
to increase overnight into Tuesday with PWATs continuing to slowly 
increase closer to 1.5". Low clouds spread from west to east with 
some scattered light showers possible.


KEY MESSAGE 2...A low pressure system will bring a prolonged period of rain
late Tuesday through Thursday, with light scattered showers 
potentially lingering into Friday. Periods of heavy rain with 
scattered instances of flash flooding are possible. 

Model guidance has stayed fairly consistent with a strong signal for 
a prolonged period of substantial rainfall accompanied by a risk for 
flash flooding. There is strong agreement across model guidance with 
a deepening mid-level trough across the Northeast Tuesday into 
Wednesday enhancing large-scale ascent over the region. Southerly 
flow will help advect in a plume of well-above normal moisture (120-
170% of normal) into the region. Precipitable water values may 
approach 1.75-2.0" by Tuesday night. A 500 mb low closes off 
generally west of the southern New England, slowly tracking eastward 
into late-week. Guidance has also stayed consistent with the 
development of a surface low pressure which will be vital with the 
magnitude and potential impacts of this robust system. Deterministic 
and ensemble guidance continues to indicate disagreement on the low 
strength and more importantly track. The tracking of the low center 
and features will likely have a strong influence on where the most 
favorable forcing is for banded heavy rain (LLJ position, 
frontogenesis). The notable spread/uncertainty across model 
solutions for the low details has translated directly to rain totals 
as well rate rates and location of bands. This creates a complex 
forecast where leveraging the full range of solutions is key 
instead of honing in on one solution. 

What is more certain is that an anomalous low pressure for late July 
tracks in the vicinity of southern New England early Wednesday into 
late-week. The cooler-season like forcing with this system combined 
with the moist, unstable warm season airmass will provide a 
favorable set-up for banded rainfall, heavy at times. Soundings 
exhibit deep moisture with sufficient warm cloud depths accompanied 
by instability. All in support of efficient rain processes and thus 
heavier rates as well. Track will also influence timing of this to 
some extent as well. Generally the rain increases from the 
west/southwest on Tue/Tue night with the greater risk of western 
locations seeing the first true push of rain in this timeframe. 
Probabilities continue to increase overnight into early Wednesday 
when the better forcing arrives. Early Wednesday through early 
Thursday is where we will see majority of the rain and potentially 
heavy rainfall/rates. As the low center rotates through it will wrap 
around additional precipitation as it very slowly moves through the 
region. This would continue rain through Thursday, potentially 
even Friday.

Across ensemble guidance rain totals range from 1.5 to 3 inches for 
most areas. The ECMWF ens leaned higher with totals compared to the 
GEFS. This has been consistent with previous runs. The placement of 
the heavier bands will be vital in where the higher totals end up. A 
more predictable mechanism that may act to enhance amounts is the 
upslope
